Let me give you the whole decision in two minutes, because half of these calls end with people still asking why. The rate moved half a point last month. The main driver is the cohort that joined in April, and it moved because that group reached its third payment. That is when a cohort tells you what it really is. We ruled out the model in the first hour, so the policy was the next place to look, and that is where we found it. Now, the part I want to be honest about. My assumption is that the root cause is a rule we loosened in March, but I do not have evidence for that yet, and I am not going to present a theory as a fact. The decision is to tighten it again. The trade-off is growth: as a result, we lose two quarters. I would rather explain two slow quarters than explain a write-off.

There is one sentence that separates the people I trust from the people I have to check, and it is I do not know. Somebody who never says it gets believed less over time, not more, because after a while nobody can tell which of their sentences are solid and which ones are decoration. So here is the habit. Put two words in front of a theory: my assumption. My assumption is that the change in March caused it. That costs you nothing, it takes half a second, and it protects everything else you said in that meeting. And one more thing, for the careful ones, because the careful ones make the opposite mistake. If you wait until the evidence is complete, you arrive at the meeting after the decision has been made. Say the theory, label it, and stay in the room.

When banks tighten their lending rules, the effect on the numbers arrives almost immediately. Lending falls within weeks. However, it takes far longer to come back than it took to fall, and in most markets it has never fully returned to where it was. The people who pay for that are not the ones anybody pictures. They are the customers who sat just above the line, because they are the first ones a stricter rule removes, and they are usually the ones with the shortest record rather than the worst one. And here is the hardest part for whoever owns the rule. The cost of tightening is visible in a month, and the benefit takes about a year to appear in the numbers. Therefore the decision looks wrong for three quarters, even when it was right, and the person who made it has to keep saying so.
